info.bio:
The Rolling Stones es un conjunto de rock británico formado en Londres en 1962. Marcaron el renacimiento del rock and roll tras el período de Elvis Presley y ocuparon un lugar importante en el redescubrimiento del blues negro.

Sus integrantes más destacados son el guitarrista Keith Richards y Mick Jagger, cantante y líder del conjunto.

own_scenes.place: Londres (Richmond, Eel Pie Island) y Hollywood
own_scenes.desc: Andrew Loog Oldham, su Svengali adolescente, los moldeó como los anti-Beatles: groseros y divisivos, «monstruos melenudos del Id adolescente» (tras la multa por orinar contra el muro de un garaje en 1965, puso a Jagger en el titular). En 1965 «(I Can’t Get No) Satisfaction», con su fuzz y su racimo final de «no», expresó una insatisfacción casi cósmica con el consumismo que los había encumbrado; Jagger, culto y elocuente en Charlie Is My Darling de Peter Whitehead, decía que el pop por fin hablaba de levantarse, ir a trabajar y sentirse jodido. «19th Nervous Breakdown» (4 de febrero de 1966), grabado en Los Ángeles al final de una gira de cuarenta fechas, fue la primera gran declaración pop del año: dos guitarras metálicas entrelazadas (Richards y Brian Jones por última vez en un single), ritmo rockabilly maníaco, casi cuatro minutos sobre una pobre niña rica sin salida. Cada single debía superar al anterior en doce semanas. Mientras se codeaban con Anita Pallenberg, Robert Fraser o Christopher Gibbs, Aftermath (abril), entero de composiciones propias, fue el LP del año, aunque en «Stupid Girl» o «Under My Thumb» el desprecio por las mujeres no inquietó a nadie.

notes.chapter: Abril: The Third Eye: el LSD y sus descontentos
notes.text: Jagger tomó LSD por primera vez en abril de 1966 en Luggala, la fiesta de veintiún cumpleaños de Tara Browne en Irlanda, «el inicio de una búsqueda de decadencia» según Marianne Faithfull. «Paint It, Black», con el sitar distorsionado de Brian Jones, expresaba una pena convertida en nihilismo casi apocalíptico.

notes.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje
notes.text: Con los Beatles retirados eran el primer grupo, pero la presión no cedía. «Have You Seen Your Mother, Baby, Standing in the Shadow?» (23 de septiembre), grabado con prisas tras una gira de treinta y dos fechas, mezcla Motown, rockabilly y pop áspero con una letra de LSD donde la amante se vuelve madre: «un apocalipsis anfetamínico en 45». La promocionaron vestidos de mujeres de los años cuarenta en las fotos de Jerrold Schatzberg y en dos películas de Peter Whitehead donde las fans, como Furias, devoran al grupo en el Albert Hall. Se quedó en el número 5: demasiado oscura, demasiado lejos, demasiado deprisa.

influences.name: Beat, R&B y mod pop británico

refs.q: This was the first big pop statement of 1966.
refs.para: On 4 February 1966, the Rolling Stones released their tenth UK single, ‘19th Nervous Breakdown’; in the US, where the band’s ‘As Tears Go By’ was still in the Top 20, it was issued a week later. The group were coming off an extraordinary run – five consecutive #1s in the UK, four Top 10 hits in the US – that saw them rivalling the Beatles in terms of perceived cultural importance, if not actual sales. This was the first big pop statement of 1966.
refs.chapter: Febrero: 19th Nervous Breakdown: la cultura adolescente británica y la locura del Swinging London

refs.q: It begins with two metallic guitars interlocking in counterpoint
refs.para: It begins with two metallic guitars interlocking in counterpoint, Richards and Brian Jones weaving together for one last time on a 45. Jagger comes in with a first verse that mixes, in equal measure, contempt, boredom and empathy. The chorus is a blare, with Jagger’s upward inflection on the repeated ‘here it comes’ underscored with foghorn guitar.
refs.chapter: Febrero: 19th Nervous Breakdown: la cultura adolescente británica y la locura del Swinging London

refs.q: This was strange: a pop star at the zenith of his fame expressing boredom and anomie.
refs.para: This was strange: a pop star at the zenith of his fame expressing boredom and anomie. Yet it tied Jagger and the Rolling Stones into how many of their audience felt and how they perceived the world. While they were fantasy figures living a life of opulence and fame, they were also subject to the same boredom, the same frustrations and the same curious dissatisfaction in the midst of comparative plenty. To that extent they were still, just about, able to be seen as ‘ordinary kids’.
refs.chapter: Febrero: 19th Nervous Breakdown: la cultura adolescente británica y la locura del Swinging London

refs.q: This was a new kind of showbiz: building up anti-heroes, with their worst characteristics amplified.
refs.para: It was a defining moment. ‘Fleet Street went ballistic over the story,’ Andrew Loog Oldham remembered in his memoir, 2Stoned, ‘so I moved Mick into the headline and the band’s image as long-haired monsters from the teenage Id was enhanced. I say “I moved” – it probably involved nothing more than me lying in the affirmative when some optimistic scribe asked whether Mick was in the front line.’ This was a new kind of showbiz: building up anti-heroes, with their worst characteristics amplified.
refs.chapter: Febrero: 19th Nervous Breakdown: la cultura adolescente británica y la locura del Swinging London

refs.para: On Aftermath, persona becomes person: the nastiness of the Rolling Stones’ constructed image spills over into the lyrics of ‘Stupid Girl’, ‘Under My Thumb’ and ‘Out of Time’. Jagger’s difficulties with his then partner, Chrissie Shrimpton – a feisty upper-middle-class girl who gave as good as she got – translate into a high level of contempt towards women that received zero comment from the male reviewers of the album and, indeed, does not seem to have troubled many of the group’s female fans at the time.
refs.chapter: Febrero: 19th Nervous Breakdown: la cultura adolescente británica y la locura del Swinging London

refs.q: ‘Paint It, Black’ was the most extreme thus far in the group’s malign mid-sixties run.
refs.para: He wrote as the Rolling Stones’ latest single was surging up the charts on both sides of the Atlantic. ‘Paint It, Black’ was the most extreme thus far in the group’s malign mid-sixties run. Signalled by Brian Jones’s distorting sitar and driven by Bill Wyman’s rumba rhythms and Charlie Watts’s slamming beats, the song expressed a grief so overwhelming that it spilled over into an angry, almost apocalyptic nihilism. Not that that was picked up by contemporary reviewers. On 14 May, Record Mirror pronounced it ‘a sad old theme’ but ‘immediately commercial’.
refs.chapter: Abril: The Third Eye: el LSD y sus descontentos

refs.q: This was an amphetamine apocalypse on 45
refs.para: ‘Have You Seen Your Mother, Baby, Standing in the Shadow?’ displays a group not entirely in control of what they are trying to do or say. Six months after ‘19th Nervous Breakdown’, the Rolling Stones are running the year’s white-line fever right off the rails. This was an amphetamine apocalypse on 45, glossed by Oldham: ‘The Shadow is the uncertainty of the future. The uncertainty is whether we slide into a vast depression or universal war.’
refs.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje

refs.q: It was an ultimate statement that failed.
refs.para: However, ‘Have You Seen Mother, Baby, Standing in the Shadow?’ was not the grand slam that the Rolling Stones and Oldham had expected. It was an ultimate statement that failed. There were several reasons: it wasn’t exactly a hummable tune, and many listeners were turned off by the all-embracing sonic murk and uncompromising darkness of tone. Even so, its comparative failure was, as Disc and Music Echo put it, ‘the most astounding shock of the financial year ending April 1967’. In the paper’s post-mortem, the Hollies’ drummer Bobby Elliott put his finger on it: ‘The record was basically above the fans’ heads. It was too hippy and those photos showing the Stones in drag put the youngsters off a bit. The Stones need slowing down.’ Manfred Mann singer Mike d’Abo thought that, unlike the Beatles, the Stones had ‘not achieved an image of being all-round family entertainers. And the image that brought them to the top now looks a bit played out.’
refs.chapter: Septiembre: 7 And 7 Is: provocaciones, sombras y un nuevo lenguaje

scenes.name: El disco
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Una simulación repetitiva de la crudeza del funk negro, alargada por máquinas y no por músicos que improvisan. Nació en clubes europeos de finales de los sesenta que pinchaban funk original, llegó a Estados Unidos y en 1974 era la moda de la Costa Este: aceleró la destrucción de la sesión en directo, de las bandas y de la grabación con alma, y la música negra se volvió más mecánica y menos significativa. El disco quería bailar sin fin sobre un ritmo único; el funk, levantarse y hacer jam («Freak of the Week»: nada de ese «disco sádico» de un solo golpe). Las bandas de funk lo atacaron («The Undisco Kidd», «Anti-Disco» de Mutiny) o se vendieron: James Brown se proclamó «Original Disco Man», los Ohio Players, los Isley y Earth, Wind & Fire («Boogie Wonderland») cayeron. El grito «Disco sucks» metió en el mismo saco a toda la música negra de baile, y muchas bandas de funk murieron por no vender como el disco.

scenes.name: MTV y Headbangers Ball
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: MTV nace en agosto de 1981 y en dos años casi monopoliza el videoclip. El heavy, visual desde que Judas Priest se vistió de cuero, es un candidato natural: entre los primeros grupos emitidos están Quiet Riot, Mötley Crüe, Twisted Sister, Dokken y Scorpions, y la cuota de mercado del metal salta del 8 % en 1983 al 20 % en 1984 («MTV fue responsable del resurgir del heavy», dice Dee Snider). A principios de 1985 la presión fundamentalista lo recorta, pero en 1988 nace el programa nocturno «Headbangers Ball». MTV selecciona del metal lo compatible con un público juvenil general: hace del lite metal un coautor del género (pelo cardado, chico malo mono, chicas en el público) y empuja al thrash, casi ausente, a definirse como antítesis comercial. Los vídeos, rodados por directores de publicidad, cuestan cada vez más (190.000 dólares uno de Poison en 1989) y dejan fuera a las bandas pequeñas, convierten los conciertos en simulacros del vídeo y, al llevar el metal al salón familiar, despiertan a sus enemigos: la lista de los «Filthy Fifteen» del PMRC y el departamento de normas de MTV.
scenes.family: Cultura metal: público, medios y conciertos

scenes.name: Fundamentalismo, pánico satánico y acoso al metal
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El metal es el último blanco de una larga tradición conservadora contra la música popular: el jazz que «causó la perdición» de mil chicas de Chicago en 1921-22, el rock and roll que el Ku Klux Klan llamaba música salvaje de negros, el folk «comunista», el rock drogado de Spiro Agnew. A finales de los setenta la derecha fundamentalista resurge justo cuando el metal crece y MTV lo mete en las casas. Se queman discos (Iowa en 1980, Saint Paul en 1981, una escuela baptista de Florida en 1982 que destruye «Hell Is for Children» de Pat Benatar, una canción contra el maltrato infantil); se buscan mensajes satánicos grabados al revés (el «experto» Wilson Bryan Key los encontraba hasta en las galletas Ritz); psiquiatras como Paul King sacan conclusiones de pacientes ingresados en sus clínicas; la policía de California usa un manual que pide censurar Creem, Hit Parader y Circus; detienen en escena a Sebastian Bach, de Skid Row, por mover la pelvis; se cancela un concierto de Metallica en Notre Dame; los colegios prohíben camisetas y hay quien quiere «desmetalizar» a los fans. Para Weinstein el satanismo del metal no es una contrateología sino un juego dionisíaco con los símbolos, heredero del blues: si la sociedad pone el éxtasis en el lado del mal, el metal se llama a sí mismo malo.

scenes.name: El diluvio: invasión británica y garage
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El Mersey-beat lleva a su conclusión la idea de los Beach Boys (ritmo de rock'n'roll y melodía pop): los Beatles, «la segunda gran estafa del rock'n'roll», popularizan lo que surge del underground. Frente a ellos, las tres grandes bandas británicas de 1964: los Rolling Stones (que redefinen al intérprete, el concierto y la canción rock y fijan el eje cantante-chamán y guitarrista carismático), los Kinks (inventores del riff más famoso y del garage, el hard rock y el heavy metal) y los Animals; los Who llevan al límite el himno generacional y la ópera rock, y los Yardbirds establecen la supremacía de la guitarra. En EE UU la invasión británica desata el garage-rock, los proto-punks de cada ciudad (Kingsmen, Sonics, Standells, ? and the Mysterians, Monks).

scenes.name: Psicodelia y acid-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: En 1965 San Francisco se convierte en la ciudad más efervescente del país: los Grateful Dead tocan en los «acid tests» de Ken Kesey, nace la escena hippy y en 1966-67 llega el verano del amor. El acid-rock, evolución del folk-rock pensada como banda sonora del viaje de LSD, es el equivalente rockero de la pintura abstracta, el free jazz y la poesía beat: su gran invento es la «jam», con la guitarra eléctrica al mando y un espíritu zen en lugar del dolor del blues. Jefferson Airplane encarnan la era; los Grateful Dead inventan la improvisación colectiva libre (Anthem Of The Sun, Live Dead); Kaleidoscope, Moby Grape, Quicksilver, Blue Cheer o Fifty Foot Hose amplían el abanico. Monterey y Sgt Pepper (1967) convierten lo alternativo en mainstream. Fuera de California, Jimi Hendrix declara la guerra a la armonía occidental con su guitarra.

scenes.name: Detroit: MC5 y Stooges
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La ciudad más industrial de EE UU y cuartel de los elementos más extremistas de la contracultura: un rock'n'roll feroz y ruidoso se convierte en la voz de los obreros y de sus hijos. Los MC5 de John Sinclair, ala revolucionaria de las revueltas estudiantiles (Kick Out The Jams, «el equivalente rockero de una explosión nuclear»); los Stooges de Iggy Pop, síntesis de Chuck Berry, Rolling Stones, Velvet Underground y Doors que inventa el punk-rock («1970») y el voodoobilly («TV Eye»). Un nuevo rock'n'roll fundado en la violencia extrema.
scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

scenes.name: Surf y garage de los noventa
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La mayor concentración de garage-rock de los noventa está en Escandinavia (Hellacopters, Gluecifer, Motorpsycho). El revival instrumental: Man Or Astroman, Mermen, Los Straitjackets, Satan's Pilgrims, Shark Quest. La herencia de los Cramps (Oblivians, Reverend Horton Heat, Gas Huffer, Chrome Cranks, Southern Culture On The Skids), la de MC5 (God And Texas, New Bomb Turks, Love 666), el Noroeste (Mummies, Mono Men, Makers, Murder City Devils) y las nuevas lecturas del blues a la sombra de Jon Spencer: Railroad Jerk, Clawhammer, Gits, Delta 72, Mule y Red Red Meat, que evolucionan hacia la deconstrucción posmoderna y luego Califone.

podcast.title: Elton Mont Speedway Free Festival Incident (1969)
podcast.body: The Rolling Stones hired the Hell's Angels motorcycle gang for $500 and all the beer they could drink to provide security for their set at the Elton Mont Speedway Free Festival on Saturday, December 6, 1969. While the band was performing "Under My Thumb," an 18-year-old named Meredith Hunter allegedly pointed a gun at the stage. In response, the Hell's Angels stabbed Hunter five times and kicked him to death, an event captured by three cameras filming the concert. This tragic incident, and the subsequent acquittal of biker Alan Pacerro on self-defense grounds (though the case wasn't formally closed until May 2005), is said to have "formally killed the peace and love vibe of the 1960s."

xref.title: Elton Mont Speedway Free Festival Incident (1969)
xref.body: The Rolling Stones hired the Hell's Angels motorcycle gang for $500 and all the beer they could drink to provide security for their set at the Elton Mont Speedway Free Festival on Saturday, December 6, 1969. While the band was performing "Under My Thumb," an 18-year-old named Meredith Hunter allegedly pointed a gun at the stage. In response, the Hell's Angels stabbed Hunter five times and kicked him to death, an event captured by three cameras filming the concert. This tragic incident, and the subsequent acquittal of biker Alan Pacerro on self-defense grounds (though the case wasn't formally closed until May 2005), is said to have "formally killed the peace and love vibe of the 1960s."

xref.title: Naked in Bed with Mick Jagger – Angela Bowie's 1990 TV Claim, Denied Then Partially Walked Back
xref.body: On May 4, 1990, David Bowie's ex-wife Angela appeared on the Joan Rivers Show, newly freed from a 10-year gag order after their divorce. She stated on national television: "I caught him in bed with Mick Jagger — and yes, they were naked." Bowie was a professed bisexual during the 1970s. Mick Jagger immediately dismissed the claim as "rubbish," and Bowie's lawyer sent an open letter stating that "any implication that there was ever a gay affair between Mick Jagger and David Bowie is an absolute fabrication." Within a week, Angela was qualifying her statement. By her 1993 autobiography, the account had evolved: she had walked in, assumed they had been having sex, and that was her honest belief, but she had no proof. An additional complication: Angela may have had her own affair with Jagger during the marriage, possibly inspiring the Rolling Stones song "Angie" — or, in another rumor, that "Angie" referred to David himself using a nickname. "Did they spend the night together? Yes. Were they naked? Apparently. Was it sexual? Who knows?"

xref.title: Initial Reluctance on Fuzz for "Satisfaction"
xref.body: When writing and recording "Satisfaction," Keith Richards used the Maestro Fuzz tone pedal to mimic a horn section for the iconic riff, intending it as a temporary placeholder. As a blues musician, he preferred a real horn section, but the rest of The Rolling Stones loved the guitar sound and overruled him. This decision led to the distorted guitar being permanently featured front and center in rock music. "Chief hated it. He was a blues guy. xref.body: Robert Smith's older siblings introduced him to a diverse range of artists, including The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, Captain Beefheart, David Bowie, Jimi Hendrix, and Nick Drake. The subsequent arrival of punk rock, with bands like Sex Pistols, Ramones, and Elvis Costello, further shaped his musical direction and helped him find his artistic niche. "His older brother and sister had filled his head with beetles and stone songs, but they also subjected him to a lot of Captain B-Fart, and David Bowie, and Jimmy Hendrix and Nick Drake. And then when punk came along, it was Sex Pistols Ramones Elvis Costello. Young Robert found his niche."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Robert Smith's Influences
xref.body: Robert Smith's musical upbringing was shaped by his older brother and sister, who introduced him to The Beatles and The Rolling Stones. They also exposed him to more unconventional artists like Captain Beefheart, David Bowie, Jimi Hendrix, and Nick Drake. The arrival of punk further influenced Smith, with bands like the Sex Pistols, Ramones, and Elvis Costello helping him discover his artistic niche. "His older brother and sister had filled his head with beetles and stone songs, but they also subjected him to a lot of Captain B. Fart, and David Bowie, and Jimmy Hendrix and Nick Drake."

xref.title: Rolling Stones Manager
xref.body: Andrew Loog Oldham was the manager of The Rolling Stones during their early career, releasing "The Rolling Stones Songbook" in 1966 which contained the orchestral arrangement of "The Last Time" later sampled by The Verve. He was later succeeded by Allan Klein. "Andrew Lou Geoldem, the manager of the Rolling Stones back in the day."

xref.title: Similarity to Rolling Stones' "Brown Sugar"
xref.body: The Dandy Warhols' alt-rock hit "Bohemian Like You" from 2000 was widely noted for its significant melodic and structural similarities to The Rolling Stones' 1971 song "Brown Sugar." "But the fact that it sounded a lot like brown sugar from the Rolling Stones did not escape attention."

xref.title: Similarity to The Rolling Stones
xref.body: The Dandy Warhols were mentioned in a context of songs sounding alike, specifically in relation to The Rolling Stones' "Brown Sugar," with the implication that no legal action was taken despite potential similarities. "Just as there was nothing involving the Dandy Warholz. And the Rolling Stones' Brown Sugar."
